topics.label: Dangerous dogs
topics.question: When is a dog “dangerous” — and what happens to you?
topics.intro: Almost every town (95%) defines a dangerous dog by what it does. A regional minority — 21%, concentrated in the South — also singles out specific breeds. Below the headline fork sits the everyday machinery: leashes, barking, head-counts, licenses.

approaches.name: Deed, not breed
approaches.blurb: Any dog that bites or threatens is “dangerous,” whatever its breed.

approaches.name: Breed-specific (BSL)
approaches.blurb: Names pit bulls or specific breeds for extra rules or outright bans.

approaches.name: Breed-neutral by law
approaches.blurb: Explicitly forbids judging a dog dangerous by breed alone.

approaches.name: Keep it contained
approaches.blurb: Leash and “running at large” rules.

approaches.name: Keep it quiet
approaches.blurb: Barking and noise nuisance rules.

approaches.name: How many
approaches.blurb: Caps on the number of dogs per household.

approaches.name: License & rabies
approaches.blurb: Registration, tags and vaccination.

approaches.name: Kennels
approaches.blurb: Care standards for keeping many animals.

laws.title: Vicious dogs
laws.plain: A dog is “vicious” if it bites, tries to bite, attacks, or physically threatens people or pets — but not if it was provoked or the victim was trespassing. The breed is irrelevant: a dog can’t be branded vicious just for being a pit bull or any other breed. A vicious dog must be kept in a secure enclosure.
laws.text: The term “vicious dog” means any animal … which bites, attempts to bite, attacks, attempts to attack, or otherwise constitutes a physical threat to humans or domestic animals, except an animal which … threatens a person or animal unlawfully upon the premises of its owner, or … which has provoked or teased it. … no dog may be declared vicious based solely on the breed of said animal. It shall be unlawful for any person to keep a vicious animal within the city limits unless the enclosure … meets the conditions …

laws.title: Dangerous dogs; registration
laws.plain: Once a court declares your dog “dangerous,” you can keep it only if you register it: pay a $50 fee, build a proper enclosure, post a warning sign, get the dog spayed or neutered, and report any new bites or change of owner.
laws.text: No person may own a dog adjudicated dangerous … unless the dog is registered … A registration fee of $50 shall be imposed … The county will issue a certificate of registration … if the owner presents sufficient evidence that: (1) A proper enclosure exists and … the premises are adequately marked with a warning sign … (2) The animal has been neutered or spayed …

laws.title: Declaration not breed-specific
laws.plain: Cullman puts the principle in a single sentence: no animal can be labeled dangerous or vicious because of its breed alone.
laws.text: No animal shall be found to be potentially dangerous or dangerous/vicious based solely on its breed.

laws.title: Pit bulls prohibited without breed-restricted permit
laws.plain: Denver singles out pit bulls. You can’t own one without a special “breed-restricted permit” — which means registering the dog and naming two emergency caretakers, among other conditions.
laws.note: Denver banned pit bulls outright from 1989 until 2020, then switched to this permit system.
laws.text: It shall be unlawful for any person to own or keep any pit bull within the city without first obtaining a breed-restricted permit … Application … shall include … the names and addresses of two (2) persons who may be contacted to take responsibility in the case of emergency …

laws.title: Ownership of pit bulls
laws.plain: Aurora names three specific breeds and puts their owners under extra rules.
laws.note: Enacted December 2024 — breed-specific laws are still being written today.
laws.text: Any owner of an American Pit Bull Terrier, American Staffordshire Terrier, or Staffordshire Bull Terrier kept as a household pet or working within the city shall adhere to all requirements in this chapter, as amended from time to time.

laws.title: Pit bull dogs
laws.plain: Cabot creates a “potentially dangerous breed” category and defines a pit bull by kennel-club breed standards — including mixes that mainly look like pit bulls — then bans keeping one except under strict conditions.
laws.text: There shall be a recognized category of dogs designated as a potentially dangerous breed. … A pit bull … is defined as any dog that is an American pit bull terrier, a Staffordshire terrier, or American Staffordshire terrier, bull terrier, and any dog of mixed breeding that has the primary characteristics … The American Kennel Club and United Kennel Club standards … shall be on file …

laws.title: Pit bulls required to be spayed or neutered
laws.plain: Lamar doesn’t ban pit bulls but requires every one to be spayed or neutered — unless it’s a young puppy, medically exempt, brand new to town, or a licensed show or breeding dog.
laws.text: It is unlawful for any person to own, keep, or harbor any dog within the city that the person … knew, or should have known, was a pit bull that has not been spayed or neutered. [Exceptions: under eight weeks of age; … cannot be spayed or neutered without a high likelihood of serious harm; … present in the city for less than 30 days; … a license to keep an intact pit bull.]

laws.title: Running at large prohibited
laws.plain: Dogs and cats can’t roam loose anywhere in the city, ever — and the same rule covers livestock and fowl. Females in heat must be confined.
laws.text: It shall be unlawful for the owner or person having charge of any dog or cat to permit or allow such dog or cat to run at large within the corporate limits of the city at any time. … Every female dog or cat in heat … shall be confined … so that [it] cannot come into contact with another animal except for planned breeding.

laws.title: Running at large to be confined
laws.plain: A loose dog or cat is a “public nuisance” the city can seize. You get five working days (and a fee) to reclaim it before it’s adopted out or put down.
laws.text: Any dog or cat found to be running at large within the city is hereby declared to be a public nuisance, and the same may be seized and confined … such animal may be reclaimed by its owner … within five working days … Any animal not reclaimed … shall become the property of the city and may be humanely euthanized or made available for adoption …

laws.title: Barking dog
laws.plain: Persistent barking, howling, or yelping that disturbs the neighborhood is illegal. A ticket needs an officer who saw it, or two complaining neighbors from different households. Barking between 10:30pm and 7:30am is presumed to be a violation.
laws.text: It shall be unlawful for an owner or keeper of any dog to fail to prevent such dog from disturbing any person or neighborhood by loud and persistent or habitual barking, howling, or yelping. [A citation must be] supported by at least two (2) identified complaining witnesses from separate households … barking … between the hours of 10:30 p.m. and 7:30 a.m. … shall create a rebuttable presumption that the dog barking was unlawful.

laws.title: Barking and howling dogs
laws.plain: Daytime barking (7am–10pm) that disturbs neighbors can be ticketed after three complaints in 90 days from at least two households — or after a warden personally hears the dog bark for 20+ minutes.
laws.text: Between … 7:00 a.m. and 10:00 p.m., it shall be unlawful for any person to keep … any dog which by loud and frequent barking or howling shall disturb the peace … Upon receiving three or more complaints … within a 90-day period, with at least two being from separate households … or … direct observation/verification … of such dog barking for more than 20 minutes …

laws.title: Maximum number of dogs
laws.plain: No household may keep more than four dogs. Vets, kennels, and licensed breeders are exempt.
laws.text: It shall be unlawful for any person or persons to own, possess, harbor or feed more than four (4) dogs upon premises owned or occupied by such person … The provisions … shall not apply to any business … which operates animal hospitals, veterinary clinics, kennels, or animal breeders …

laws.title: Limitation of number of cats and dogs
laws.plain: No more than four cats and/or dogs combined (over four months old) per home. A fifth is allowed for up to 30 days with permission; beyond that you need a kennel permit.
laws.text: No person shall keep, harbor or maintain upon his premises … more than a total of four cats and/or dogs combined over the age of four months [unless] … permitted to keep a fifth cat or dog for a period … not to exceed thirty (30) days; [or obtains] a yearly kennel permit.

laws.title: Registration and vaccination
laws.plain: Every dog and cat must be registered with a local vet, vaccinated for rabies, and renewed yearly. The rabies certificate doubles as the city tag; the fee is $3.
laws.text: All city residents who own and maintain dogs or cats … shall register their dog or cat with a local licensed veterinarian. Upon registration, the animal(s) shall be vaccinated for rabies … The certificate shall serve as the city registration tag … valid for one (1) year … A registration fee of three dollars ($3.00) …

laws.title: Standards for kennels
laws.plain: Kennels must meet basic care standards: weatherproof, washable enclosures; comfortable temperature and ventilation; room for each animal to stand, lie down, and turn around; and clean, dry, sanitary runs.
laws.text: Enclosures must be provided which shall allow adequate protection against weather extremes. … Each animal shall have sufficient space to stand up, lie down and turn around without touching the sides or top of cages. … All animal quarters and runs are to be kept clean, dry and in a sanitary condition.

topics.label: Fireworks
topics.question: Can you set off fireworks in your own backyard?
topics.intro: Towns answer this four ways — and the answer is shaped heavily by state law. Where a state bans consumer fireworks, its cities stay silent; where the state allows them, nearly every city writes its own rule.

approaches.name: Banned
approaches.blurb: No consumer fireworks at all.

approaches.name: Holiday windows
approaches.blurb: Allowed only on set days — July 4th, New Year’s.

approaches.name: Public displays only
approaches.blurb: Pros can get a permit; you can’t.

approaches.name: Regulate the sale
approaches.blurb: Stands, zoning and age limits.

laws.title: Fireworks prohibited
laws.plain: You can’t sell, use, or set off any fireworks in Dillingham unless the city manager personally grants permission.
laws.text: It is unlawful for any person within the city to sell or use or explode any fireworks, explosives or stench bombs to which fuses are attached or which are ignitable by means of a match, without permission of the city manager or designee.

laws.title: Fireworks, explosives, stench bombs
laws.plain: Fireworks are banned year-round except two windows: 10pm July 3 through midnight July 4, and 4pm New Year’s Eve through 8pm New Year’s Day. No sales to anyone under 18, and never set them off dangerously or while drunk.
laws.text: Use of fireworks is prohibited at all times except from ten p.m. on July 3rd to eleven-fifty-nine p.m. on July 4th, and from four p.m. on December 31st to eight p.m. on January 1st of each year … The sale of fireworks to any person under the age of eighteen is prohibited.

laws.title: Fireworks displays — permission required
laws.plain: Public fireworks displays for special occasions are allowed — but only with written permission from both the police chief and fire chief, who must be satisfied it’ll be safe. Backyard use isn’t covered.
laws.text: The borough chief of police and fire chief are granted the joint authority to permit any person to give a fireworks display for any special occasion … but no such … display shall be conducted without first securing permission in writing from the chief of police and the fire chief …

laws.title: Temporary fireworks stands
laws.plain: Seasonal fireworks stands are allowed in certain commercial and industrial zones, with parking and setback rules — the town regulates the selling, not just the setting-off.
laws.text: Temporary fireworks stands are permitted by right in C-2, M-1 and M-2 zoning districts, subject to … setback requirements … [and] a minimum of five off-street parking spaces … per fireworks stand.

topics.label: Backyard chickens
topics.question: Can you keep backyard chickens?
topics.intro: About half of all city codes address chickens or other fowl — the single biggest coin-flip in local law. The ones that do pick one of three approaches.

approaches.name: Banned
approaches.blurb: No fowl inside city limits, period.

approaches.name: Farm zones only
approaches.blurb: Fine on agriculturally-zoned land, nowhere else.

approaches.name: Allowed, with conditions
approaches.blurb: Setbacks, coop standards, often hen caps and no roosters.

laws.title: Fowl prohibited
laws.plain: In Florence it’s flatly illegal to keep any fowl — chickens, turkeys, guineas, even peacocks — anywhere in the city.
laws.text: It shall be unlawful for any person, within the corporate limits of the city to keep or have in his possession any fowl. [“Fowl” = any large, live domestic birds including … chickens, guineas, turkeys, homing pigeons … ostrich, and peacocks.]

laws.title: Fowl only in agricultural districts
laws.plain: You can keep fowl only on land zoned agricultural, and they must be securely enclosed. A loose bird is automatically treated as proof your enclosure isn’t good enough.
laws.text: It shall be unlawful and shall constitute a public nuisance … to keep or maintain such animal or fowl in any zoning district other than the one zoned for agricultural use … The running at large of any … fowl shall be prima facie evidence that the enclosure … is not constructed and maintained according to the requirements …

laws.title: Distance of fowl enclosures from dwellings
laws.plain: Birmingham allows fowl but with rules: no coop within 100 feet of a home, church, school, or park, and at least 15 square feet of space per bird. Separate sections require ventilated coops and ban birds from running loose.
laws.text: It shall be unlawful for any person to keep … any … chicken … in any … enclosure … any part of which is within 100 feet of a dwelling, church, hospital, school, public building, public park or public thoroughfare. There shall be provided for each fowl … a minimum of 15 square feet of space …

topics.label: Noise
topics.question: How loud is too loud? Two very different ways to write the rule.
topics.intro: Some towns set a line you can measure; others leave it to judgment. Noise is the cleanest example of “bright-line vs. discretion” — the very split LOCUS scores as enforcement discretion.

approaches.name: Decibel limit
approaches.blurb: A number you can check with a meter.

approaches.name: Plainly audible
approaches.blurb: Illegal if heard from X feet away — no meter needed.

approaches.name: “Unreasonable”
approaches.blurb: Judged by factors: time, duration, place.

approaches.name: Quiet hours
approaches.blurb: Banned during set night-time hours.

laws.title: Noise — 80 dBA limit
laws.plain: Between 11pm and 6am, no sound may exceed 80 decibels measured at your property line. It’s an exact, meter-checkable limit.
laws.text: No loud noise … shall be permitted within this land use district during the hours from 11:00 p.m. to 6:00 a.m. “Loud noise” is defined as a decibel level that exceeds eighty (80) dBA max at the property line of the parcel … receiving the noise.

laws.title: Sound plainly audible at 25 feet
laws.plain: It’s illegal to play audio so loud it’s “plainly audible” 25 feet away. No decibel meter required — the test is simply whether an officer can hear it from that distance.
laws.text: It shall be unlawful for any person to play, use or operate … any radio … or other machine … for reproducing sound … in such a manner that the sound generated is plainly audible at a distance of twenty-five (25) feet or more from the source of the sound.

laws.title: Standards for unreasonable noise
laws.plain: Instead of a number, Hot Springs lists what an officer weighs: how loud, what time of day, how long, whether it keeps happening, whether it’s necessary, and how close to homes. It’s a judgment call, not a measurement.
laws.text: The standards which may be considered in determining whether a violation … exists may include … (1) The level or volume of the noise. (2) The time of day or night … (3) The duration … (4) Whether the noise is recurrent, intermittent or constant. … (8) The proximity of the noise to residences …

laws.title: Noise-making devices at certain hours
laws.plain: Loudspeakers, sound trucks, and amplified music are banned in public from 11:30pm to 8am — and all day Sunday.
laws.text: It shall be unlawful to use any device known as a sound truck, loudspeaker or sound amplifier, or radio, television or phonograph with a loudspeaker … which emits … loud and raucous noises on the streets and sidewalks of the city … from the hour of 11:30 p.m. until 8:00 a.m. and on Sunday.

topics.label: Short-term rentals
topics.question: Can you list your home on Airbnb?
topics.intro: A genuinely modern fork — most of these rules were written in the last few years. Towns license, zone, set operating rules, or restrict.

approaches.name: License & tax
approaches.blurb: Register, pay a fee or lodging tax, name a contact.

approaches.name: Zoning & caps
approaches.blurb: Occupancy limits, parking, where it’s allowed.

approaches.name: Operating rules
approaches.blurb: No signage, no exterior changes, minimum stays.

approaches.name: Restrict
approaches.blurb: Bar it, or leave HOA bans in force.

laws.title: Short-term rentals — licensing
laws.plain: Before you can even advertise, you need a city STR license — one per property — and you must name an emergency contact who answers complaints within an hour and can show up on-site within 12 hours.
laws.text: The property owner must have a valid short-term rental license from the city before a property can be advertised or operated … [and] provide … the name and telephone number of an emergency contact that will respond within one hour to complaints … [and be] able to respond on-site within 12 hours if requested …

laws.title: Short-term rental business license
laws.plain: Auburn treats an Airbnb like a business: an annual license costing one-quarter of one percent of your rental income, at least $100.
laws.text: An annual business license fee is hereby fixed at an amount equal to … one-fourth (¼) of one per cent (gross receipts × .0025), provided that the minimum business license fee shall be one hundred dollars ($100.00) … 1. Short term non-primary rental … 2. Homestay …

laws.title: Short-term rentals — use criteria
laws.plain: Jasper caps occupancy at two people per bedroom plus two, bans any signage advertising the rental, requires an up-to-code permanent building, and forbids serving food to guests.
laws.text: The building … must meet all applicable building codes, fire codes … No on-site signage identifying the property as a short-term rental is permitted. … Occupancy … is limited to two persons per bedroom, plus two additional persons. The licensee may not prepare/serve food to rental guests.

laws.title: No physical changes to the home
laws.plain: Your rental has to keep looking like a house — you can’t, say, add a separate guest entrance just for renters.
laws.text: Short-term rentals may not result in physical changes to the home so that it no longer looks like a home, such as constructing a separate building entrance for the sole use of the renters.

laws.title: Short-term rentals — generally
laws.plain: You can’t run a short-term rental without following the city’s rules — and the city explicitly leaves any HOA ban on STRs in force.
laws.text: It shall be unlawful for a person to rent any portion of a dwelling unit to a transient without complying with the provisions of this article. The provisions … shall not supersede the prohibition of short-term rentals by a homeowner’s association …

regionalNotes.snow_removal: Pure climate. South Dakota (100%), Iowa, Minnesota and Wisconsin almost all make property owners clear their sidewalks; Louisiana, Georgia and Florida have essentially none. It snows, or it doesn’t.
regionalNotes.fireworks: Often decided one level up. New Jersey, New York and Massachusetts ban consumer fireworks statewide, so their cities rarely need a rule (16–20%). Where the state allows them — Arizona, Iowa, North Dakota — nearly every city writes its own (90–100%).
regionalNotes.marijuana: Follows legalization. Colorado and California cities overwhelmingly address marijuana (88–96%); in states that never legalized, like Indiana and Idaho, city codes are silent.
regionalNotes.curfew: A regional culture line. Juvenile curfews are routine in the Midwest and Appalachia (Ohio 90%, West Virginia 76%) and rare in the Northeast (New Jersey 5%, Massachusetts 8%), where they’ve faced more legal pushback.
regionalNotes.dangerous_dogs: Nearly universal as a behavior-based rule — but the breed-specific version (banning pit bulls by name) is a Southern signature: Mississippi, Arkansas, Louisiana and North Carolina lead, while most of the country relies on breed-neutral “dangerous dog” laws.
regionalNotes.golf_cart: Rural-road culture. Common where golf carts and ATVs share local streets (Iowa 76%, West Virginia 65%) and absent in dense states (Maryland, Massachusetts 0%).
regionalNotes.loitering: An Appalachian and Midwestern staple (West Virginia 91%, Ohio 86%); rare in the upper Midwest and Mountain West, partly because loitering laws draw constitutional challenges.
regionalNotes.chickens: A near coin-flip nationally, tilting rural. Roughly half of city codes regulate fowl; the share climbs in farm states and falls in the dense Northeast.
regionalNotes.open_burning: Tracks wildfire risk and air rules — commonly permitted with a seasonal permit in rural areas, banned outright in dense or fire-prone ones.
regionalNotes.peddlers: Door-to-door selling is one of the oldest licensed trades; prevalence is high in the South and industrial Midwest, low where newer codes fold it into general business licensing.
